title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

findings.claim: The painkiller aspirin was originally derived from willow bark
findings.explanation: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) was synthesised from salicylic acid, not directly from willow bark. The active compound salicin was first isolated from willow bark in 1828 (Buchner), then salicylic acid was obtained in 1838, and acetylsalicylic acid was first synthesised by Gerhardt in 1853 and commercialised by Bayer in 1899. Saying aspirin was 'derived from willow bark' is a GCSE-level simplification widely used in textbooks, but it elides the synthetic chemistry step. The lesson does not say 'extracted from' but 'derived from', which is defensible at GCSE. Minor concern only.

findings.claim: The antibiotic penicillin was discovered from a mould by Alexander Fleming in 1928
findings.explanation: Correct. Fleming observed Penicillium notatum (now P. rubens/chrysogenum) inhibiting Staphylococcus cultures in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital, London. Date and attribution are accurate.

findings.claim: The heart drug digitalis comes from foxgloves
findings.explanation: Correct. Digitalis compounds come from Digitalis purpurea (common foxglove) and Digitalis lanata. William Withering described its use for dropsy in 1785. Digoxin was isolated from D. lanata in 1930.

findings.claim: Vaccines introduce a small quantity of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen and stimulate white blood cells (lymphocytes) to produce antibodies
findings.explanation: Correct at GCSE level. Vaccines can use dead/inactivated or attenuated pathogens. They stimulate lymphocytes (B-cells) to produce antibodies and generate memory cells.

findings.claim: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is an example of a superbug resistant to several antibiotics
findings.explanation: Correct. MRSA resists methicillin and the wider beta-lactam class. It is widely described as a 'superbug'.

notes: Solid lesson. The aspirin claim is a well-established GCSE simplification, acceptable at this level.

title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum

findings.claim: In a vacuum, all EM waves travel at the same speed — the speed of light: c = 3 × 10^8 m/s
findings.explanation: Correct. The exact value is 299,792,458 m/s; the 3 × 10^8 m/s approximation is standard for GCSE.

findings.claim: Visible light ranges from red (longest visible wavelength, about 700 nm) to violet (shortest, about 400 nm)
findings.explanation: Correct. Visible spectrum: approximately 380–700 nm (violet to red). The 400 nm lower bound is a reasonable GCSE approximation.

findings.claim: A diode only conducts in one direction. There is a threshold voltage (about 0.6 V for silicon) below which even forward current is negligible
findings.explanation: 0.6 V is commonly cited for silicon at GCSE level; the more precise engineering value is 0.65–0.7 V. Both 0.6 V and 0.7 V appear in authoritative GCSE resources. This is within acceptable GCSE tolerance.

findings.claim: Radio waves can induce oscillations in electrical circuits; when electrons oscillate in a transmitter aerial at a certain frequency, they generate radio waves at that same frequency
findings.explanation: Correct. This is the standard explanation for radio wave generation and reception at GCSE/A-level.

notes: Well-constructed lesson with accurate physics. The 0.6 V silicon diode threshold is a minor low-severity simplification consistent with GCSE standards.

title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid

findings.claim: UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz
findings.explanation: Correct. UK nominal supply is 230 V (±10%/–6%) at 50 Hz per the Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002.

findings.claim: Live wire (brown) alternates between about +325 V and −325 V
findings.explanation: Correct. Peak voltage = 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V. This is the correct peak-to-peak calculation.

findings.claim: The live wire is dangerous even when the switch is off, because it is still at 230 V relative to earth
findings.explanation: Correct. The live wire maintains 230 V (rms) potential difference relative to earth regardless of the appliance switch position, since the switch is in the live wire between the live terminal and the appliance.

findings.claim: Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and low currents
findings.explanation: Correct. The UK National Grid uses 400 kV and 275 kV transmission lines.

notes: No factual errors found. All key claims verified against authoritative sources.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

findings.claim: Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged elements in order of atomic weight but left gaps for undiscovered elements and swapped some elements so that those with similar properties lined up in the same columns. When elements such as gallium and germanium were later discovered and matched his predictions, his table was widely accepted.
findings.explanation: Correct. Mendeleev presented his table in 1869, left gaps, and his prediction of gallium (discovered 1875) and germanium (1886) confirmed the table. The lesson accurately states these key features.

findings.claim: Going down Group 1, the elements also have lower melting points and higher densities going down the group
findings.explanation: The melting point part is correct (decreases down Group 1). The density claim ('higher densities going down the group') is an oversimplification: density generally increases, but there is a well-known anomaly at potassium, which has a lower density (0.89 g/cm³) than sodium (0.97 g/cm³). At GCSE level this trend is often stated without the potassium exception, but stating it as absolute is imprecise. This is a minor accuracy concern — GCSE mark schemes typically accept the general trend.

findings.claim: Group 7 (halogens): Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to gain an extra electron
findings.explanation: Correct. As atomic radius increases down the group, the incoming electron experiences less nuclear attraction and more shielding, reducing reactivity.

findings.claim: Transition metals — iron in the Haber process
findings.explanation: Correct. Iron (specifically alpha-Fe/ferrite) is used as the catalyst in the Haber process.

notes: One low-severity oversimplification: the Group 1 density trend stated without the potassium anomaly exception. Acceptable at GCSE level but worth noting.

title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

findings.claim: Light microscopes were first developed in the 1590s
findings.explanation: Correct. The compound microscope is attributed to Hans and Zacharias Janssen in the late 1590s (a 1595-dated specimen bearing the Janssen name is held at Middelburg museum). Attribution is debated but the 1590s date is the standard GCSE claim.

findings.claim: Light microscopes: max magnification ≈ ×1,500, resolution ≈ 200 nm
findings.explanation: Correct. These are the standard GCSE/A-level figures, consistent with diffraction-limited visible light optics.

findings.claim: Electron microscopes: max magnification ≈ ×2,000,000, resolution ≈ 0.2 nm. The development of electron microscopes in the 1930s was a turning point
findings.explanation: Correct. Ernst Ruska built the first practical electron microscope in 1933 (the first electron lens was 1931, commercialised 1939). The 1930s attribution is accurate. Resolution ~0.2 nm and magnification ×2,000,000 are standard GCSE figures.

findings.claim: Red blood cells: has no nucleus, leaving more room to carry haemoglobin
findings.explanation: Correct. Mature mammalian red blood cells (erythrocytes) lose their nucleus during differentiation.

notes: Accurate lesson. All key claims verified.

title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection

findings.claim: Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection to explain how evolution occurs
findings.explanation: Correct. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, proposing natural selection as the mechanism for evolution. (Alfred Russel Wallace co-developed the theory; omitting Wallace is a common GCSE simplification, not a factual error.)

findings.claim: Carl Linnaeus developed the classification system that organises living things into groups based on shared characteristics: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
findings.explanation: Partially inaccurate. Linnaeus's original system used kingdom, class, order, genus, species — it did not include phylum or family. Those ranks were added by later taxonomists. However, the full seven-rank hierarchy is now universally attributed to 'Linnaean taxonomy' in educational contexts, so this is a GCSE-standard simplification rather than an outright error. The attribution to Linnaeus of the seven-rank system is standard in GCSE biology textbooks.

findings.claim: Evidence for evolution comes from: fossils, antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and comparative anatomy
findings.explanation: Correct. All three are standard lines of evidence for evolution in GCSE biology.

notes: The Linnaeus seven-rank taxonomy claim is a common GCSE simplification, not a serious error. Overall an accurate lesson.

title: Bonding

findings.claim: Ionic bonding occurs between metals and non-metals
findings.explanation: Correct at GCSE level. Ionic bonding typically occurs between metals and non-metals via electron transfer.

findings.claim: A double bond forms between two oxygen atoms (O₂) and a triple bond between two nitrogen atoms (N₂)
findings.explanation: Correct. O₂ has a double bond (two shared pairs) and N₂ has a triple bond (three shared pairs). These are standard molecular structures.

findings.claim: In metals, outer-shell electrons are delocalised — free to move through the whole structure — leaving a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons
findings.explanation: Correct. This is the standard description of metallic bonding.

findings.claim: Giant covalent structures include diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide
findings.explanation: Correct. All three are giant covalent (macromolecular) structures with covalent bonds throughout the lattice.

notes: No factual errors found. Well-structured and accurate chemistry lesson.

title: Equilibria

findings.claim: The decomposition of ammonium chloride: NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g). When heated, ammonium chloride breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases. When cooled, these gases recombine to form solid ammonium chloride again.
findings.explanation: Correct. This is a standard reversible reaction example. The equation and description are accurate.

findings.claim: The forward reaction is exothermic (absorbs energy) — wait, the lesson says 'The forward reaction is endothermic (absorbs energy); the reverse reaction is exothermic (releases energy)'
findings.explanation: Correct for ammonium chloride decomposition. Thermal decomposition of NH₄Cl is endothermic (absorbs heat). The reverse (recombination) is exothermic. The lesson has this correct.

findings.claim: Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). Conditions: ~450°C, ~200 atm, iron catalyst. Only about 15% conversion per pass; unreacted gases are recycled.
findings.explanation: All claims correct. ΔH = −92.4 kJ/mol (cited as −92, which is a common rounding). 450°C and 200 atm are standard GCSE figures. ~15% single-pass conversion and gas recycling are accurate.

findings.claim: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally
findings.explanation: Correct. Catalysts lower activation energy equally for both directions, increasing the rate at which equilibrium is reached but not the equilibrium position itself.

notes: Highly accurate equilibria lesson. All chemical facts and Le Chatelier applications verified.

title: Static Charge and Simple Circuits

findings.claim: When a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons move from the cloth to the rod: the rod becomes negative and the cloth becomes positive
findings.explanation: Correct. Polythene has a higher affinity for electrons than the cloth (usually wool or cotton), so it gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.

findings.claim: Strictly speaking, Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature remains constant
findings.explanation: Correct. This is the standard statement of Ohm's law with its temperature condition.

findings.claim: An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot
findings.explanation: Correct. NTC thermistors decrease in resistance with increasing temperature. The lesson correctly identifies the NTC designation and behaviour.

findings.claim: A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has high resistance in the dark and low resistance in bright light
findings.explanation: Correct. Standard GCSE description of LDR behaviour.

notes: No factual errors found. Accurate physics lesson.

title: Evolution and Classification

findings.claim: Ardi (Ardipithecus ramidus) dates from about 4.4 million years ago. Ardi had both ape-like features (long arms, an opposable big toe for gripping branches) and human-like features (she could walk upright on two legs, at least some of the time).
findings.explanation: Correct. Ardi is dated to 4.4 million years ago. She had a mosaic of features: ape-like opposable big toe and long arms, but evidence of bipedal walking. All claims verified.

findings.claim: Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) dates from about 3.2 million years ago. Lucy had a smaller brain than modern humans but her skeleton shows she walked upright more efficiently than Ardi. Her knee and hip joints were adapted for bipedal walking, showing that walking upright evolved before large brains.
findings.explanation: Correct. Lucy is dated to 3.2 million years ago. Her anatomy confirms more efficient bipedalism than Ardi, with still a small brain. The 'walking before large brains' conclusion is a standard and well-supported paleoanthropological claim.

findings.claim: Richard Leakey's discovery from about 1.6 million years ago (often called Turkana Boy) was a nearly complete skeleton of Homo erectus.
findings.explanation: The fossil is real and the dating (1.6 mya) is correct. However, the actual discoverer of Turkana Boy was Kamoya Kimeu (on 1 August 1984), a member of Richard Leakey's team, not Leakey personally. Turkana Boy Wikipedia article, the Leakey Foundation, and Turkana Basin Institute all credit Kimeu as the finder. Calling it 'Richard Leakey's discovery' is a common attribution shorthand in educational materials (and the Edexcel GCSE spec itself often phrases it this way), but it is not strictly accurate. The lesson follows the Edexcel curriculum wording, so this is a curriculum-level issue rather than a content error.

findings.claim: Scientists now use the three-domain system: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya. Carl Woese proposed the three-domain system in 1990.
findings.explanation: Correct. Woese, Kandler, and Wheelis formally proposed the three-domain system in 1990, designating Archaea, Bacteria, and Eucarya (Eukarya).

findings.claim: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is an example of a bacterium that has evolved resistance to several antibiotics
findings.explanation: Correct. MRSA is resistant to the entire beta-lactam class and often other antibiotic classes.

notes: The Turkana Boy attribution to Richard Leakey personally (rather than Kamoya Kimeu) is a common curriculum-level simplification that appears in the Edexcel specification itself. No HIGH severity issues found.
